title: 10,500-year-old wooden remains in German lake
dek: Underwater archaeologists found worked timbers and stone tools at Lake Arendsee.
body: About 20 metres beneath Lake Arendsee in Saxony-Anhalt, underwater archaeologists have uncovered 10,500-year-old worked timbers, stone tools and animal bones. The discovery emerged during spring 2026 investigations of submerged prehistoric landscapes by the State Office for Heritage Management and Archaeology of Saxony-Anhalt. Researchers recovered large and small pieces of worked wood alongside animal remains linked to hunting.

Among the most striking finds is a wooden post roughly 1.6 metres long that preserves clear evidence of felling and working. Split wooden planks measuring up to 1.3 metres long were also recovered. Researchers suspect the timbers may have belonged to a constructed feature, potentially even a hut. Yet no building plan or other evidence has yet established that the wood formed part of a dwelling.

Describing the site as a permanent settlement remains premature. The finds demonstrate that Mesolithic people were active at the former lakeshore and were working substantial pieces of timber there, but further investigation is required to determine the nature and duration of that activity. Around 10,500 years ago, communities in Central Europe relied on hunting, fishing and gathering rather than agriculture.

Even if a structure is eventually identified at Arendsee, this would not necessarily indicate permanent occupation. Hunter-gatherer communities could construct substantial features at camps or other locations that were occupied temporarily or revisited seasonally. The importance of the discovery instead lies in the exceptional survival of worked wood from the Mesolithic period.

Evidence for structures from this period is often preserved only indirectly, through features such as postholes and changes in soil colour. The waterlogged environment at Arendsee has preserved the timber itself, including traces of prehistoric woodworking. A salt dome beneath the lake has caused sections of the lakebed to gradually submerge former shorelines, and subsequent sediment covered archaeological remains along these ancient shores.

The lake has already produced discoveries from several periods, including Neolithic fish weirs and medieval watercraft. Researchers are now using underwater technology to investigate the prehistoric landscape in greater detail. A remotely operated underwater vehicle, deployed in collaboration with researchers from the Fraunhofer Institute in Ilmenau, has produced high-resolution sonar imagery of the former shoreline.

Researchers hope to conduct dendrochronological analysis using the surviving tree rings, although dating such ancient wood is challenging because suitable comparative material is scarce. The timbers are also expected to undergo magnetic resonance imaging in Halle to reveal additional information about their internal structure. Further dives will attempt to establish the extent of the archaeological remains and determine whether the individual pieces of worked wood were connected.
doesnt_show: The evidence does not yet confirm a permanent settlement or identify the function of the worked wood.
settle: Targeted dives establishing whether the timbers belong to a connected structure or separate activities will determine the site's function.
